faqs.question: When do the new CGT rules take effect?
faqs.answer: The new CPI indexation rules and 30% minimum tax floor take effect from 1 July 2027, provided the legislation passes parliament. This is not yet law — it requires a Senate vote.

faqs.question: I already own an investment property. Am I affected by the negative gearing changes?
faqs.answer: If you owned the property (or had a contract signed) before 7:30 PM on Budget Night (13 May 2026), you are fully grandfathered. Your negative gearing deductions remain exactly as they are today.

faqs.question: Is my SMSF affected by the new CGT rules?
faqs.answer: No. Self-Managed Super Funds are completely exempt. They retain the existing one-third CGT discount and are not subject to the 30% minimum tax floor.

faqs.question: What is CPI indexation and how does it work?
faqs.answer: CPI indexation adjusts your asset's cost base for inflation. If you paid $100,000 for shares and inflation has been 2.5% per year for 10 years, your adjusted cost base is approximately $128,000. You only pay tax on the real gain above that — not the inflation component.

faqs.question: What is the 30% minimum tax floor?
faqs.answer: It means your effective tax rate on net capital gains will never fall below 30%, regardless of your total income. Previously, retirees could time asset sales to low-income years and pay very little CGT. The floor closes this strategy.

faqs.question: Can I still negatively gear a new investment property?
faqs.answer: Yes. New builds (newly constructed residential properties) retain full negative gearing regardless of when you buy. The restriction only applies to established (pre-existing) homes purchased after Budget Night.

faqs.question: What happens to shares I bought before the 1985 CGT exemption date?
faqs.answer: If you hold assets purchased before 20 September 1985, their full CGT exemption ends on 1 July 2027. The ATO will establish a new cost base via market valuation on that date. Any gains after 1 July 2027 will be taxed under the new CPI indexation rules.

faqs.question: Are these changes definitely going ahead?
faqs.answer: Not yet. Budget announcements are proposals, not law. They must be legislated through parliament. The Opposition has flagged a Senate challenge. Always speak to a registered accountant before making financial decisions based on these changes.

faqs.question: How does inflation indexation affect CGT calculation?
faqs.answer:
The 50% CGT discount — which allowed taxpayers to halve their net capital gain before adding it to taxable income — is being replaced with inflation-based cost base indexation.

Under the new system, your asset's purchase price is adjusted for CPI inflation from the date of purchase to the date of sale. This means only the real purchasing power gain is taxable, not gains that merely track inflation. For example, if you bought shares for $50,000 and CPI rose 40% over your holding period, your indexed cost base would be $70,000 — even if the nominal gain was larger.

Comparing the two approaches: The 50% discount provided a consistent benefit regardless of how long you held the asset. Inflation indexation grows more valuable the longer you hold, but only up to inflation. For assets held through low-inflation periods, the discount may have been more generous.

The 'bunching' concern: The Australian Shareholders Association has noted that inflation indexation does not fully address income bunching — where investment gains accumulated over many years are all realised in a single tax year. A taxpayer who holds an asset for 20 years and sells it in one year will have all CPI-indexed gains taxed in that single year, potentially pushing them into a much higher tax bracket. Industry groups are calling for a capital gains averaging mechanism to smooth tax liability across multiple years, similar to how income averaging works for artists and authors. This has not been legislated.
